entry.title: The revolution will look like a campus
entry.summary: Using the idea of a "campus" as a model for little bubbles of semi-autonomy. If you can't do a big revolution, why not a small one?

div.p: Recently, I've struggled to reconcile my usual optimism with the landscape that I'm seeing. The post-revolution world I dream of seems impossibly far away sometimes, with turnout to actions dwindling as tiredness sets in. Incremental change is torturously slow, and the people don't seem primed for revolution. But as I've talked about before, I see some of the most valuable revolutionary acts to be the creation of "bubbles" that block out the usual forces of policing and governance, giving us brief footholds. In this post I want to expand on that idea.

Wikipedia summarizes its page on "campus" as "…the land and buildings of a college or university, or a company's office complex." A campus is usually a collection of buildings, although it could just be one building, or a collection of disconnected spaces spread across buildings shared for other purposes. In addition to the productive spaces that facilitate the campus's direct purpose, like classrooms or offices, it will usually also provide for some or all of the occupants' survival needs. Water fountains and restrooms are always present. Most university campuses have dormitories for students. Institutions of all types will often have some form of dining facility. Large campuses might have gyms, medical clinics, chapels, prayer rooms, libraries, public transit stations, cross-campus shuttles, cafés, grocery stores, athletic fields, or more.

A campus is often livable for long periods of time. While a corporate office campus is unlikely to include housing or intend to accommodate for overnight stays, those are the exception compared to colleges, hospitals, and military bases. A campus often provides a much higher standard of living than a city or suburb, due to its density and opportunities for socialization. Many have written about how much of the uniqueness of "the college experience" can actually just be attributed to the benefits of living in such a space.

Most definitions you'll find will associate campuses with institutions of some sort. In our current world, that's not surprising; it's rare for hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of people to organize themselves into a dense cluster of spaces optimized for a certain objective without some hierarchical structure overseeing them. But my idea with this post is that a campus without an institution is not only possible, but a promising direction for some sort of revolution.

Imagine living on something roughly shaped like a college campus. In a small footprint, you'd have densely packed living spaces (probably apartments rather than dorm-style or semi-suite rooms); gardens and green spaces; workspaces (offices, studios, workshops); restaurants or dining halls; libraries; water bottle fillers and restrooms; gyms; medical clinics; stores; and other spaces that facilitate survival, socialization, or advancement of human pursuits.

If the campus is relatively self-contained, its inputs and outputs can be discussed without worrying about how resources are distributed within. The inputs would likely include food (minus whatever can be grown within the space), water, energy (whether in the form of electricity or the fuels used to produce it), non-food grocery items, office and hobby supplies, construction materials for growth or repairs, medical supplies, and raw materials for anything produced within. The outputs (aside from trash, recycling, and sewage) would include money and labor to purchase the campus's inputs, and any outgoing mutual aid to surrounding communities.

The ability to abstract the inputs and outputs of the campus at large is powerful. If occupants have relatively little business to do with the outside world, the distribution of resources — including currencies used — in that outside world would not necessarily need to govern how they're distributed within the campus. Trust-based distribution of resources and labor is difficult to scale, but the boundaries of the campus provide a cell-like semi-permeable membrane that allows the people within it to act like a small, discrete system while still benefiting from trade with the rest of the world (and its capacity for specialized manufacturing, which no small isolated group of people could possibly replicate).

People within the campus would still work, probably about as much as they would otherwise. Some percentage of that work would be within the campus, doing whatever gardening and cottage industry is worth doing internally, and the rest of it would be in the outside, capitalist world. How the money from that labor flows into the campus might be a little difficult to work out, but it'd be reasonable for some of it to go into the campus's shared financial resources, and some of it to remain with the worker. The defining distinction between mutual aid and charity is that mutual aid builds infrastructure that gives us a systemic advantage in the fight against capitalism, while charity just moves money around. The campus, with its scale and sources of comparative advantage, would be among the strongest forms of mutual aid: able to spend the proportion of money that one person (or family) spends on basic survival in a manner far more efficient than the individual could, without middlemen like landlords and consumer-facing retailers that skim margins off of goods they buy wholesale.

Once a non-institutional campus like this is set up, it would provide a foothold for disruption of the status quo. Unlike an isolated commune, it would be in direct contact with a surrounding urban (or suburban) population, with inflow and outflow of people and information. It could (and should) fill the functions of a school, public co-working space, library, food pantry, hospital, and defensive outpost. Once multiple are formed, they'd be able to offer aid to one another, and basic specialization could start to occur (some things aren't worth buying two of if you know someone else who has one). Universities are already able to supplant most of the functions of local government for their students; a large, sophisticated non-institutional campus could do the same.
div.h2: A certain means by which one could potentially acquire a campus
div.p: If you're sold on the vision, you might now be wondering how we kickstart this whole process. Building a bubble of a couple thousand community-minded people with its own land, buildings, and (limited) production capital might be easier than bringing a whole nation to the brink of revolution, but it still takes assets and organization that we don't currently have just sitting around. Luckily, we don't need to do all that work ourselves. Turns out, campuses are pretty easy to find!

Colleges and universities continue to be on the front lines of radical political organizing in the US. Colleges and universities also tend to come with beautiful, already-built campuses that students, staff, and faculty — the people — are thoroughly familiar with, more so than their admins (walled away in their towers as they are), and certainly more than local police and national guard. Many school campuses become so complex that first responders can't be trusted to navigate them under normal circumstances (prompting the creation of campus police and EMS services). You might call that an excuse for the slow creep of fascism into our most vulnerable spaces, but I call it a tactical advantage!

Unlike city blocks and suburbs, schools also have relatively high turnover and little sense of ownership. Students stay for four years or so, then they're expected to leave. Staff and faculty often move frequently as well. It's not anyone's permanent home, and whatever corporations are allowed to set up shop typically don't have as permanent of a presence as local businesses. If anarchists can take over a city neighborhood for days to weeks, that's good progress, but they're like lichen clinging to rocks. Flat surfaces and shallow buildings can be swept quickly, and forces will continue to desire the right of return for the petty bourgeoisie for decades to come. But a college campus is well-connected, deep physical space: it's hard to flush out people who have controlled the space long enough to fortify it and make it their own. We would be like pinecones sprouting in the blackened earth after a wildfire.

The ready-made campus approach would come with its own issues compared to the more sanctioned routes for building a non-institutional campus, of course. It might be harder to do business with companies on the outside, for example, and getting stable employment to provide the campus with income could be riskier. It would be more ideal if a large group could all put down their life savings and buy or build a cluster of buildings near a city, but if it was that easy to liberate ourselves from the unmitigated brunt of capitalism, more people would have done it. Us youths are more radical than our parents' generations, and a number of the US's colleges aren't contributing to the world quite as positively as one would hope, so it might in fact be time to toughen up a little and take a bolder approach.

entry.title: Why I wrote "free Palestine by any means necessary" on The Fence
entry.summary: Why I wrote "free Palestine by any means necessary" on The Fence, intended for CMU and my hearing officer to consider as part of the investigation into my June 9th Fence painting.

div.p: This is a long, but hardly thorough, description of why I wrote "free Palestine by any means necessary" on The Fence, intended for CMU and my hearing officer to consider as part of the investigation into my June 9th Fence painting. In the interest of good faith, I am also posting its precise contents on my public blog, so that it's clear I'm not filtering who I am or what I believe when showing myself and my world to CMU for this inquiry. Most of this is context intended to put myself and whoever it is who's reading this on the same page. It's a difficult task, seeing as this is the most divisive issue of our time, one where information, history, and words themselves are front lines bitterly fought for.
div.h2: What is Palestine? What is Israel? (Who are Palestinians? Who are Israelis?)
div.p: To start us off, I'm going to define how I use some words and phrases, so that (ideally) nothing I write later is misunderstood. First off, I'm going to draw a distinction between regions, states, and nations.

A region is a piece of land, neutrally, usually without hard borders. Regions can overlap, and regions can go by many different names. Depending on which name someone uses for a region, you can sometimes get a sense for how they view that land in a political or cultural context, but typically the region itself is not something with politically contentious boundaries. You and I could fight a war for control over, say, Appalachia, but it stays in roughly the same place no matter who controls it and what wars are fought over it.

In this document, I'm mostly going to talk about one region. Roughly, that region is the land east of the Mediterranean Sea, mostly west of the Jordan River, mostly north of the Sinai Peninsula, and mostly south of Lebanon and Syria. Don't focus too much on those as precise boundaries. Historically, the neutral term for that region is "Palestine," and it's the term you'll find in encyclopedias. In the case of Wikipedia, there's distinct pages for "Palestine" (the state) and "Palestine (region)". As the latter article states, "[o]ther names for part or all of this region include Canaan, the Promised Land, the Land of Israel, the Holy Land, and Judea." None of those are in common use to describe precisely the same region, and "Palestine" is widely accepted as the neutral term for the region, so that's what I'll use.

A state, for the purposes of this document, is a political entity with sovereignty, a government, policing, and defined borders which it defends. (I'm not a geographer or a political theorist, but I think that definition should be serviceable.) Unlike regions, states cannot overlap.

In the region of Palestine, there are roughly two states: (the state of) Israel and (the state of) Palestine. I say "roughly" because, unlike regions, it is a political question whether something is a state or not, and the statehoods of both Palestine and Israel are contentious on the world stage. When I say "Palestine" or "Israel," I will be explicit if I'm referring to a state rather than a region or nation.

Lastly, a nation, for the purposes of this document, is a group with a common identity with a tie to a region. Like regions themselves, nations do not have hard borders, and can overlap in physical space. Since nations are composed of people rather than land, nations can be distributed far across the world, and individual people can consider themselves parts of multiple nations. All that must be true is that those people all have a shared identity associated with that nationality, and that the identity is tied to some region.

At least two nations have strong ties to Palestine (the region), under this definition. One group, the one we're usually talking about when we say "Palestinians," describes Arabs native to the region of Palestine. Although Palestine has gone through numerous wars and upheavals over centuries, there is a strong Palestinian cultural identity associated with the region. At the start of the 20th century, Palestinians were some 90% of the population of the region, but millions have been displaced since 1948.

The other group you could describe as a nation with strong ties to the region of Palestine would be whichever nation that Israel, the nation-state, is intended to correspond with. This is complicated, because Israel, the state, is built on the idea that Jewish people collectively form one nation, tied to Palestine. Judaism originated in Palestine, and a Jewish population has lived in Palestine since antiquity, but the idea that Palestine is a homeland for the whole of the Jewish people is not a universal idea. In practice, many Jewish people do not claim Palestine as a region that their identity is uniquely built around, and Israel has its own cultural identity (though, being quite young for a country, some criticize its originality). In practice, when people say "Israeli," they almost always are describing the citizens of the state of Israel rather than any sort of standalone nation, so I will do the same.

The concept of the "nation-state" describes a state which occupies the same physical space that a nation is rooted to. But more than that, since its introduction, the concept of nation-states has brought with it an assertion that states and nations should correspond in a one-to-one relationship. If nations did not overlap, this might work beautifully: if I have a tie to a piece of land, a tie that I share with thousands, millions, or billions of others, along with similar culture and identity, it would be lovely for us to be recognized as the proprietors of that land, for us to defend for ourselves and govern in accordance with our shared ideals. But, nations do overlap, and states cannot.

When two nations overlap (as is the case at basically any point on the surface of the planet), the idea of nation-states fall apart. Both nations might be comfortable living in the same state (or with no state at all), which is ideal, unless more nations overlap and disagree. But if just one of the nations wants its own state (or worse, both), then issues arise, and usually war.
div.h2: What is going on in Palestine?
div.p: From the middle ages to World War I, Palestine was under Ottoman control. It was mostly Palestinian Arab. Broken down by religion, it was mostly Muslim, with a Christian population of about 10% and a small Jewish minority. It was largely (though not fully) safe for people of all Abrahamic religions. Around the start of the 20th century, a political movement formed around the idea of creating a Jewish state in Palestine. Calling itself Zionism, the movement was upfront about its goal of colonizing Palestine, acknowledging that it would have to displace the native Palestinian population.

During the course of World War I, Britain issued the Balfour Declaration of 1917, describing its intent to support the Zionist project. For Britain, which would assume control of Palestine at the conclusion of the war, supporting Zionism was a strategic move, not one motivated by solidarity with the Jewish people.

After World War II and the Holocaust, the United Nations decided that Palestine would be partitioned. Following a year of civil war, 700,000 Palestinian Arabs were violently displaced and dispossessed of land and belongings, including through massacres of civilians and the use of biological warfare. This is known as the Nakba. On top of Palestinians' homes, farms, and towns, the state of Israel declared its independence.
Over the following 75 years, the number of displaced Palestinians swelled into the millions, and civilians continued to be killed in the tens of thousands.

Following October 7th, 2023, which killed around 800 Israeli civilians, over 70,000 Palestinians have been directly killed by Israel. No schools or hospitals in Gaza still stand untouched by bombs. It is well-documented that Israel intentionally targets medics and journalists. Around 80% of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces are civilians, and 20–30% are children.

I recognize that this presentation is not unbiased. If you already know about the history of Palestine and Israel, or you pay attention to news or political discourse surrounding Palestine and Israel, you may largely agree with this framing, or strongly object to it. If it's the latter, I do think you are wrong, but my goal isn't to try to change your mind in a handful of pages. I will do my best to write in a way that accommodates a variety of worldviews.

Regardless of which side, if any, you consider yourself to align with, you will understand the depth of violence and horror which has been inflicted in Palestine. Hundreds of thousands of cumulative civilian deaths is an unfathomable number. It is difficult to imagine huddling in a bomb shelter as blasts shake the ground and cake concrete dust on your skin, no matter which side of the border you personally imagine yourself sheltering in. I personally think of the young children who have lost parents in Palestine. I think of medics and journalists who grew up aspiring to save lives and bring truth to light, and who died by sniper bullets or double-tap drone strikes. I think of the men and women who have faced torture and sexual assault at the hands of so-called Defense Forces. Maybe you feel deeper pain thinking of Israeli hostages, or young adults at a rave being shaken out of their music-induced dissociation by gunfire. If so, you still undoubtedly understand the depth of the pain and trauma that has come from the violence in Palestine, the region.

In spite of its initial purpose, the state of Israel does not increase the safety of the Jewish people. The bombing and starvation and settler violence inflicted on Palestinians incites violence against the soldiers and civilians of the occupying state. The borders sit as permanent scars. None of this is necessary. The splintering of the land into two states is unnecessary. Jews, Muslims, and Christians can live side by side. People of all races can live side by side. Living side by side does not mandate violent occupation, or segregation. It is possible to migrate without colonizing, without injury to those who already live there. It is possible to build a multiracial democracy which is safe for Jewish people. For fuck's sake, that's what all of us should aspire to, in all places!

When we say "Free Palestine," that is not a call for Palestinians to do the same thing to Israelis that Israelis did to Palestinians. You can't undo the damage of colonialism using the tactics of colonialism. "Free Palestine" is a call for a number of things, like the right for Palestinians to return to the homes and towns they were displaced from and dispossessed of, but it is first and foremost motivated by grief and rage for lives lost for a concept, for lines on a map. The "Free Palestine" part of my "Free Palestine by any means necessary" is a statement fundamentally opposed to violence.
div.h2: What is the history of the phrase "by any means necessary"? Why did I use it?
div.p: If "Free Palestine" is as opposed to violence as I say, it might seem contradictory to pair it with "by any means necessary," a phrase which, interpreted literally and outside of any historical context, could be construed as a declaration of support for limitless violence. But I did not choose those words out of thin air.

When Malcolm X spoke the words "freedom by any means necessary," it played into his already-controversial public image. The next February, after acknowledging his controversial reputation, his eulogy would ask, "Did you ever talk to Brother Malcolm? Did you ever touch him, or have him smile at you? Did you ever really listen to him? Did he ever do a mean thing? Was he ever himself associated with violence or any public disturbance? For if you did you would know him. And if you knew him you would know why we must honor him."

Malcolm X would die without seeing the freedom he spoke so defiantly to secure. In poems and reflections written after his death, a recurring theme is that what struck you listening to Malcolm X, just as much as his controversial words, was his unapologetic dignity: a strength and confidence which he did not ask permission for, but instead built for himself. Maybe Malcolm X did say those words imagining his listeners taking up arms against their oppressors. But what I take from his words when I see them, and what so many writers describe in his time, is not a directive to fight one particular way or another, but instead a reminder that we do not have to run, hide, or fight according to the rules we impose on ourselves.

When you're a college student, just some kid, who chooses to bear witness to the depths of the world's suffering and oppression, you're confronted by unbearable powerlessness. How can you study in a bubble of fern-green lawns and Kittanning brick towers for four years, a drop in the ocean, while people are dying? You find yourself caught in a sort of fight-or-flight instinct. You can run from the world's problems, or try to shoulder them, desperately battling the guilt and trauma of failing to save the world. When you're boxed in like that, those controversial words don't say "fight a violent campaign of resistance," because you don't have a violent resistance campaign to fight. You have picket signs to paint, and a Student Government to bother, and classmates to inform, and skills to pick up, and friends to care for, and those are the means you have, and they are necessary. The hard way to fight isn't with guns; you can put a 17-year-old through a couple weeks of training and have a soldier. But it takes guidance from the strongest people in history to stare down forces you are near-powerless to stop for year after year, doing the "any means necessary" that you have available.

I hope that when most of my classmates saw "free Palestine by any means necessary," they too were jolted out of their flight response. I hope they thought about the means that they couldn't bring themselves to wield: scrolling through a news article, flipping through a dense book, having a hard conversation, holding a sign alone outside the University President's office, organizing a painting on The Fence, bringing a group of classmates to a protest.

So, was it anti-Jewish or anti-Israeli to paint "free Palestine by any means necessary" on The Fence? No, as I've described above. But, to go a step further, those words are the opposite of confrontational toward my Jewish or Israeli classmates. My Fence painting standing up for Palestine was directly inspired by Jewish resistance to injustice, particularly in Palestine.

When I need strength to continue fighting for things I believe in, when it becomes difficult as it inevitably does, I have a few places I tend to look. I've discussed some of those already, like the history and notable figures of the Black Power movement. But another one of those places is the continuing work of Jewish organizers, writers, and thinkers. In his short book "That precious strand of Jewishness that challenges authority," Leon Rosselson reflects on the intersections of Jewish identity, injustice, persecution, and resistance. He describes historical Jewish resistance to chattel slavery, 20th-century Fascism, and apartheid, among other grave injustices. He is clear in describing those not just as actions taken by people who happened to be Jewish, but as acts of solidarity thoroughly intertwined with, urged on by, Jewishness. "I thought of my parents' teaching that Jews should always be on the side of the oppressed," Rosselson writes at one point. "Sara Roy writes that to her parents, who were Holocaust survivors, Judaism meant bearing witness, raging against injustice and forgoing silence. It meant compassion, tolerance, and rescue. And there's this from Isaac Babel: I am a Jew because of my unconditional solidarity with the persecuted and the exterminated." (Sara Roy is a Jewish scholar and pro-Palestinian advocate, and Isaac Babel was a Russian [and later Soviet] Jewish writer executed by the NKVD.)

To be clear, I'm not Jewish. I came to CMU after living the first 18 years of my life in a suburb in the South, where I never once met someone who described themself to me as Jewish. In the two years since arriving as a blank slate, I've seen firsthand the precious strand of Jewishness that Rosselson described — I've seen it in the protests where Jewish Pittsburghers show up to loudly side with the oppressed, to use their physical presence to scream out "not in our name." I've gone to the occasional Shabbat dinner or Klezmer concert. I've read dozens of books and hand-folded zines — some long and dry, some short and punchy, some beautiful and vivid, nearly all containing songs. I have not seen a Jewishness which would cower from "freedom by any means necessary," I have seen a Jewishness which has the unique strength and moral clarity to carry centuries of tragedy and persecution not as a burden to silently shoulder, but instead a well of resilience with which to nurture hope in the moments when fighting back for one more second seems more than the spirit can bear.

entry.title: Cavitation damage as an analogy for insurrectionary anarchism
entry.summary: A short analogy comparing protests like the Capitol Hill Autonomous Zone and the Gaza Solidarity Encampment, both of which peacefully displaced policing from a physical space, to cavitation, which is a phenomenon in fluid dynamics. I then reflect a bit on how this analogy would project a slow victory for the anarchist cause. (Assumes working knowledge of anarchist thought.)

p.i: Note: If you're not familiar with anarchism (as an ideology, not just "chaos" or "the concept of not having a government"), the viewpoint in this post probably won't make much sense. I recommend To Change Everything, an anarchist appeal by CrimethInc (PDF) or Ungovernability by Tom Nomad (PDF) as good introductions to the subject.

div.p: This is a much shorter blog post than my last one, but I wanted to capture an idea that I had the other night. If you're unfamiliar with the concept of cavitation, it describes a phenomenon in fluid dynamics that can damage mechanisms like propellers and pumps. If you think about a propeller spinning underwater, it pushes a ship forward by creating high pressure on one side and low pressure on the other. But if the pressure gets low enough (say, if the propeller is spinning incredibly quickly), the water will boil into bubbles of water vapor before it can rush in to counteract the low pressure. When those bubbles collapse, it produces a shock wave that can damage the mechanism. While thinking about the Columbia encampments last night, I thought of an analogy comparing those encampments to cavitation bubbles: tiny voids in the usual pressure of "law and order," voids which are violently collapsed from the outside. I wanted to draw out that metaphor a little bit in this post, as a way of highlighting how seemingly inconsequential moments of resistance against policing can slowly do damage to the vast structures of control that are otherwise immovable through our day-to-day actions, and how that damage comes through the state's own hand.

Last night, I was watching The Encampments, the documentary about the 2024 Gaza Solidarity Encampment at Columbia University and other pro-Palestine encampments that sprung up at universities around the same time. Watching the footage in the film, I saw a bubble of peaceful solidarity. Students in the encampment were playing instruments, distributing food, painting, singing, dancing, and collectively making critical decisions. It was only where the encampments brushed up against the world outside that violence was able to sustain itself, and ultimately the encampments were suppressed through gratuitous use of state violence. It felt similar to descriptions I've heard of CHAZ, the Capitol Hill Autonomous Zone formed in 2020 in Seattle, which managed to survive several weeks before being shut down by police. Amid the usual, constant pressure from the systems of control around us, these little bubbles offer a short-lasting glimpse of a world where they are absent.

But when the cavitation bubble collapses, things do not return to precisely how they were before. After the ping of the shockwave against steel, a tiny pit is left behind, and over time, that pitting can destroy even the strongest materials. The beauty is that it isn't the vacuum left behind by the absence of water that does the damage, it's the water itself, violently surging in to crush the bubble of vapor. When the police brutalize college students to destroy a peaceful encampment, or when fascist non-state actors drive a car or fire a bullet into an autonomous anarchist zone, they themselves are doing damage to the surfaces our society acts upon. For many people, the legitimacy of policing itself is called into question when video emerges of a non-violent 19 year old in a scarf being shoved to the ground, or shot with rubber bullets, or sprayed with chemical agents. The overwhelming disparity in use of violence between the pro-human-rights crowd (whether they're anarchists, communists, social democrats, or somewhere else on the spectrum of progressivism) and the anti-human-rights crowd (whether they're police, far-right militants, university administrators, or some other form of opponent to the progressive/socialist/anarchist cause) speaks for itself, gradually destroying the legitimacy of the state in all of its forms.

It will become harder before it gets easier. With every pocket of ungovernability, every cavitation void, comes a stronger and better-equipped adversary. The 2024 occupation of Hind's (Hamilton) Hall looked much different from the 1968 occupation (where it became Malcolm X Liberation College). The state, and universities (as tiny models of the state), have access to new technologies, have developed new tactics, and have received new forms of authorization and legitimacy. But as slowly as it is happening, the tide is turning against states. Just through the issue of Israel and Palestine alone, hairy questions about the legitimacy of states and concept of the nation-state have been raised to a broad audience, and that broad audience is coming around to the answers that anarchists and other revolutionaries have known all along. Party communism may be on the rise again, but a three-arrows sort of politics has become mainstream among those progressive of the Democratic Party. The pipeline from democratic socialist to anarchist is short, far shorter than the one from democratic socialist to Marxist-Leninist. It's too early to take anything close to a victory lap, but it may be the case that in fascism's dying gasp, we are seeing a renaissance, one which will bring us closer than ever before to a fatal crack in the facade of the state.

entry.title: Distributed refuge and religious poverty: some thoughts on home and community
entry.summary: Some rambling on two concepts which inform how I think about home, community, and anti-authoritarian movements. The first is sort of the concept of livable or friendly spaces in hostile or unfamiliar places, and the second is the idea of religious poverty (which is quite distinct from material poorness).

div.p: During the Battle of Britain in WWII, aircraft were frequently shot down over the English Channel. For pilots carrying out night raids or operating in bad weather, that was a likely death sentence. As a result, both the Brits and the Luftwaffe deployed small floating shelters built to provide downed pilots with beds, dry clothes, food, first-aid supplies, and small sources of comfort like cigarettes and playing cards. Both countries' designs for these rescue buoys were about 4 square meters, and able to fit up to 4 people. Doesn't this evoke a strange feeling of homeliness? In an environment almost entirely inhospitable to human life — dark waters under an active warzone — there were tiny oases of safety and comfort, placed by an entity of almost unimaginable scale. I've always been a little obsessed with this concept of livable or friendly spaces in hostile or unfamiliar places, but I've never had a word or phrase to describe it. I figured I'd coin such a phrase and ramble about how it ties into my own somewhat unusual sense of "home" and how it's influenced by power structures (or the lack thereof).

The term I've started using for the concept behind the feeling that those WWII rescue buoys evoke in me is "distributed refuge." To give it a baseline definition, it consists of a place, providing a sense of safety and comfort, which is:

ol.li: …in an inhospitable, unfamiliar, or hostile environment, and,
…put in place by a force, body, or movement far larger than any one person.

div.p: I believe every part of this definition is important, though I have weaker examples which are missing individual elements of it.

One of the first times I remember experiencing the powerful emotional association I have with this concept was when I first read the Harry Potter series. Specifically, in book 4 (the Goblet of Fire), in which a tent is described which is much bigger on its inside than its outside. It's described as looking from the outside like a shabby 2-man tent, but on the inside as being warm and full of well-worn furniture and having a bathroom and a kitchen and smelling like cats. That space provided safety and comfort — that is to say, refuge — in a space that was hidden, in an unfamiliar campground, and through a force (magic) which was much larger than Harry or the reader and which neither Harry nor the reader had previously known possessed the power to create such refuge in the manner it did. Thus, it's a decent example of distributed refuge. (It's very unfortunate that one of the clearest examples of the idea in my mind is in Harry Potter of all places, given the significant harms against trans people that its author, Joanne Rowling, continues to fund and publicly support. As difficult as it is to boycott a series of books that was so important to my childhood, I've done so since high school and would encourage anyone reading this to do the same.)

The concept of distributed refuge is strongest for me when it encompasses all aspects of livability, including a place to sleep. Unfortunately, few examples hold up to this stronger requirement, so many of the other examples I have are weak or partial. For example, consider the eduroam wi-fi roaming service. For those who haven't used it, eduroam is a wi-fi network which is present on many secondary school and college campuses worldwide. Anyone with internet access at any one of those institutions has internet access at all of them, providing oases of a very limited form of refuge.

My dad converted to catholicism some time in his 40s, while I was a teenager. Part of his reasoning for doing so stuck with me: as he put it, wherever in the world he went (or at least, wherever a relatively closed-minded white man would want to go), there would be a catholic church not too far away, with the same services and beliefs he could expect anywhere else on the planet — in a sense, the same refuge. While catholic churches tend not to be hidden or subtle, they do fit the other two criteria, particularly with regards to being put in place by an institution far larger and older than any single person.

As a final and slightly more fantastical example, the concepts of secret societies and movie-style spies produce this same feeling for me. I used to idly daydream about starting some sort of powerful secret society distributed all across the world, so that wherever its members find themselves, and whatever trouble they find themselves in, they can get assistance from a powerful network of trusted strangers. Similarly, in spy movies, the protagonists will often need an assist in some far-flung location. One call to their handler will produce an "asset in West Berlin," or some such trusted individual wherever and whenever they need it most.

A common thread you'll have noticed is that all of these involve hierarchical, often oppressive power structures: militaries, churches, governments, etc. And this makes sense, given the third characteristic in my definition: the refuge being put in place by something far larger than oneself. The actors that are most capable of distributing aid and support across massive geographical areas are institutions which are centralized and built around a clear in-group. Without centralization it would be difficult to distribute the burden of constructing and maintaining the infrastructure of refuge (whether physical or social), and without a clear in-group it's difficult to classify a place as broadly "hostile" or "unfamiliar," and difficult to justify constructing it using private funds. Such centralized sources of refuge typically also necessitate policing or surveillance in some form or another; otherwise, they may become useful to squatters, runaways, nonbelievers, an opposing faction, or whoever the maintainers consider undesirable.

But I think there are useful counterexamples to the trend of distributed refuge as a sole output of oppressive hierarchies. For example, I find a bit of refuge every time I'm passing through an area of a city and notice antifascist graffiti. It's not necessarily confined or hidden, but it is often located in areas that might be prone to attracting the things I consider hostile and unfriendly — policing and surveillance — and a sign that those forces have not prevailed. While it isn't produced by any sort of centralized group or hierarchy, it's still maintained by a movement much larger than myself, in which the local anarchists, skater kids, or other graffiti artists also play a part. Mutual aid networks often fill two or three of the criteria for distributed refuge. Even libraries, which are products of government funding, are typically hostile to fascism and friendly to the downtrodden, making them a distributed form of comfort, safety, and predictability in unfamiliar or unforgiving locales. Maybe the greatest example of distributed refuge as a decentralized project working against oppression was the Underground Railroad, which neatly fits all three criteria.

I think the concept of distributed refuge is useful in understanding the appeal of certain hierarchical power structures, the sort that any anarchist, anti-authoritarian, or socialist project should aspire to topple. If it's possible to maintain distributed refuge without centralization and in-groups, we should seek to do so, across the domains of physical shelter, food, medicine, physical comfort, psychological comfort, and social connection. Being part of the chaotic and decentralized movements against oppression in all its forms should feel at more times than it currently does like being part of something immense and tangible and bigger than yourself, like floating warm and dry in a buoy in dark, frigid waters, and like laying the groundwork for that same refuge for future generations of fighters.

A related concept which has majorly influenced my idea of homeliness is that of Jesuit poverty. The Jesuits, which still exist but are most notable as a historical organization, are an order of Catholic missionaries. Jesuits are sworn to a life of poverty, which is used in a specific way to describe a concept separate from the typical notion of "poverty" as material poorness. Instead, Jesuit poverty is focused around owning minimal personal possessions, instead receiving resources from their surrounding community. Nothing material should tie a religious missionary down, the logic goes, so one vows against owning a dwelling, car, or valuables which cannot easily be donated or traded away should duty call. In place of personal possessions, the ideal of Jesuit poverty is that the missionary's possessions are one with their community's. Everything which the Jesuit owns is owned so that they may be of service to their community, and everything which they own is in turn provided to them by that community. Therefore, the ideal adherent of Jesuit poverty is secure, comfortable, and materially rich, but as a function of a surrounding church and community, which may continue to hold onto such resources should the missionary depart with nothing but the essentials for travel.

The idea of Jesuit poverty (or religious poverty more generally) is one I learned about long after adopting its core tenets myself, as best as one can without ties to a broader religious order. My first apartment when I moved out of my parents' house as a rebellious high school senior was rented in my own name (as well as that of my awesome roommate, who I should mention is cool and awesome), but I knew from day zero that I would not have rented it if the only person it was saving was myself. Neither I nor my initial roommate could have moved out independently. The smallest possible community is two, and for a short time that is what we were, with our two-bedroom apartment, communal fridge, and jobs at the same grocery store. The second smallest possible community is three, which we became shortly after when another of my close friends lost her already-unstable housing situation. I had known, and secretly hoped, that various friends of mine might escape the houses they lived in and find shelter under my and my roommate's roof. Other sizes of community include four and five people, each of which the apartment was at various times. We sometimes fought of course, but by and large, we lived together, shared a great deal of things, and found refuge from the bitterness of our familial relations. Quietly, and contentedly, I shouldered a much bigger financial burden than I admitted to. It wasn't a noble self-sacrifice or anything; I knew I had a much stronger support system, I had limited need to save up for college, and I had access to more sources of income thanks to some sketchy freelance coding work. I still was anchored down pretty strongly to that apartment, and I bought plenty of things for specifically myself, but the idea grew in my mind of seeing my own spaces and my own possessions as borrowings from a community to which I might, someday, be called to give them back.

Once I made it to college, and through my mandatory year in an assigned first-year dorm, I found the concept of owning and paying for a dorm or apartment for myself sort of unconscionable. Instead, I slept on couches scattered around the campus academic buildings all summer, moving when the security guards noticed my preferred spots, and showering in an abandoned locker room. When my sophomore year started, I moved into a more permanent home: an unused office in a tucked-away administrative wing of one of the campus buildings. Once I put my student status on pause for some time and was forced to move out, I finally and reluctantly found an apartment, which is where I am currently. I feel very weird about it, although for my remaining time in college, it's likely my only option. At least I can use it as a storage space for an ever-increasing stash of supplies for activism.

The core ideas behind religious poverty are, as I alluded to earlier, primarily associated with militaries and organized religions. As our social and political structures are currently organized, living as a function of one's community isn't an intended possibility. The forces of capitalism and individualism more or less force you to work for a company or government for money, to pay for and own (or rent) your dwelling and possessions using that money, and to further entrench yourself into that cycle as the only path to stability and relative comfort. But in contrast, life in the military fits those ideals rather closely: you live on a base or in barracks, you work to serve the greater aims of the nation it (supposedly) fights for, and you're kept ready to deploy to the other side of the country or the world, leaving behind your dwelling, possessions, and personal relationships to fight for the cause you've been called to.

As with distributed refuge, while religious poverty is closely tied to centralized, hierarchical, and oppressive institutions, it's just as applicable to tight-knit groups fighting for some form of social or political change. I believe that for anarchist, anti-authoritarian, or socialist projects to be successful, it would be beneficial to consider how a microcosm of community-based "poverty" can be constructed within the broader systems of capitalism, democracy, and the nation-state, while maintaining the security and comfort to sustainably live, work, and fight. Those who choose such a life — whether alone or with friends, partners, or families — could move past individualism without first having to restructure all of society to accommodate the ideal conditions for strong community-driven movements for change, which would otherwise be a circular dependency difficult or impossible to break out of.

Both of these concepts, distributed refuge and religious poverty, share important similarities. They both relate to a desire for a force or movement or organization much bigger than oneself, a desire which feeds into both hierarchical institutions and decentralized liberatory movements. They're both intimately tied to housing: anyone who's walked aimlessly alone late at night without a place to sleep has probably experienced a longing for some covert source of shelter and comfort and privacy, and anyone who's felt more at home in a movement of some sort than any physical dwelling likely understands the ideas behind religious poverty. I am a product of both of these experiences, and in my group of friends and acquaintances I can often see similar sentiments expressed (my acquaintances being, of course, a biased sample). In our current society individualism is given a strong preference over community. The notions of "home" we are given are the home as one's castle, the white-picket fence dream of a world built for the white, suburban middle class. The notions of "community" we are given are weak and insubstantial, more about socializing together than surviving together. Community is constructed as something one partakes in separately from the core necessities of shelter or comfort. Giving alternative notions of home and of community a place within our broader society without first having to destroy and rebuild it from the ground up is the only feasible option; no revolution is coming to save us.
